title: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy
author: Brandon Roberts
content:
A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into
whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics
laws after a recent ProPublica investigation [revealed actions experts called
“alarming”](https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-alicia-jackson-menopause-
treatment-policy) and an “obvious conflict of interest.”

Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health,
publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement
therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause
treatments.

[In a letter to the department’s inspector
general](https://campaignlegal.org/sites/default/files/2026-11/Jackson%20-%20208%20and%20EIGA%20Complaint.pdf),
the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified
up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm.
The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments
in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.

Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical
technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though
health officials have not publicly explained why.

In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center [cited the ProPublica
investigation](https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-alicia-jackson-
menopause-treatment-policy) that found Jackson spoke at an [HHS press
conference](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rtvhshHADM0&t=1030s) last November
and was [quoted in a department news release](https://www.fda.gov/news-
events/press-announcements/hhs-advances-womens-health-removes-misleading-fda-
warnings-hormone-replacement-therapy) announcing the decision to remove “black
box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.

At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of
stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone
replacement treatments, [according to her financial
disclosures](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/jackson-
alicia/?_gl=1*t8g1nm*_ga*OTYyNTAwNjkzLjE3NTkyNjI1Mjc.*_ga_K9RW8M6GL5*czE3OTQ1MzY3NzgkbzUzNCRnMCR0MTc5NDUzNjc3OSRqNTkkbDAkaDA.#6_9086_20).

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2269811584.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1) **Top
U.S. Health Official Backed a Medication Policy Shift That Benefited a Company
She Has Stock In** ](https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-alicia-jackson-
menopause-treatment-policy)

It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the
requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal
safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA
panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson
became her agency’s director in October 2025.

Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees
from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could
influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press
conference or in a news release.  

The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether
Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither
Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest
waiver before participating in the policy announcement.

“Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made
to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote.

The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to
fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in
private investment funds.

ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband
owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do
not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds
managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by [her husband,
Alex Jacobson](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jacobsonalex/). The company invests
in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and
medical device companies.

Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the
underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency.  

![Two men in sport jackets stand in front of a wall with the name “137
Ventures” on it.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2281096509.jpg?w=752)137 Ventures founders
Alex Jacobson, left, and Justin Fishner-Wolfson Kimberly White/Getty Images
for 137 Ventures

The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of
those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a
virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides
hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms.
Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black
box warning announcement, the center said.

Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like
Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But
Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago —
remain uncertified.

HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is
investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly
100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 [party-line
vote](https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1191/vote_119_1_00655.htm).
President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the
president’s second term.

ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137
Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS
spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the
facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials
to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”

Jackson was[ appointed by Trump as her agency’s second
director](https://arpa-h.gov/about/people/alicia-jackson) and sworn in on Oct.
20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary
biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued
numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines
combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-
related illnesses.

Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to[ ProPublica’s Trump
Team Financials database](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-
financial-disclosures/), a searchable tool launched in March. The records
detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since
last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and
the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased.
